quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct conclusion.
quests.passage: In January, the Delgado family's monthly grocery bill averaged $420. In March, after their teenage son joined the varsity swim team, his coach recommended a higher-protein diet to support training. By May, the family's grocery bill averaged $580, though gas prices had also risen slightly that spring.
options: Rising gas prices are definitely the sole explanation for the higher grocery bill. Such a pattern would remain constant throughout the scenario being described.
The family's grocery bill decreased after their son joined the swim team. This pattern would hold steady across the entire situation the passage lays out.
The son's diet recommendation had no possible connection to the family's spending. Nothing in the passage suggests this changed at any point during the period described.
The son's new diet plan is a plausible contributor to the higher grocery bill, though not the only possible factor.
quests.correctAnswer: The son's new diet plan is a plausible contributor to the higher grocery bill, though not the only possible factor.
quests.hint: Track the timeline of events and note that the passage mentions more than one change happening around the same period.
quests.explanation: The timing of the diet recommendation lines up with the rising grocery bill, making it a plausible contributor, though the mention of rising gas prices shows other factors were also part of the picture that spring.
logicChain: January: $420 average bill -> March: son starts high-protein diet -> May: $580 average bill, gas prices also rose -> diet is a plausible contributor, though not the only factor mentioned

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct conclusion.
quests.passage: Two years ago, the small architecture firm Voss & Kline had six employees and completed about four projects a year. Last year, they hired three new architects and invested in new 3D modeling software. This year, the firm completed eleven projects, and client satisfaction survey scores rose from 3.8 to 4.6 out of 5.
options: The firm completed fewer projects this year than two years ago.
Client satisfaction scores fell after the firm hired new architects. Nothing described in the passage points to any exception to this pattern.
The added staff and new software may together have contributed to the firm completing more projects with higher client satisfaction.
The new software was purchased before the firm had any employees. This reading would hold true across the full sequence of events described.
quests.correctAnswer: The added staff and new software may together have contributed to the firm completing more projects with higher client satisfaction.
quests.hint: Track the timeline of hiring, software investment, and the resulting changes in output and satisfaction.
quests.explanation: Both new hires and new software were added before the jump in completed projects and rising satisfaction scores, supporting both changes as plausible contributors to the firm's improved performance.
logicChain: Two years ago: 6 employees, ~4 projects/year -> last year: 3 hires, new software -> this year: 11 projects, satisfaction 3.8 to 4.6 -> hires and software appear to have contributed to the improvement

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct conclusion.
quests.passage: Before 2022, the small town of Millbrook had no public transportation, and most residents drove to the nearest city thirty minutes away for work. In 2022, the county introduced a shuttle bus running twice daily between Millbrook and the city. By 2023, local surveys showed 30 percent of commuters had switched from driving to riding the shuttle, and traffic congestion on the connecting highway had noticeably eased during rush hour.
options: The new shuttle service appears to have reduced highway congestion by shifting some commuters away from driving.
Traffic congestion on the highway increased after the shuttle was introduced.
No residents of Millbrook changed their commuting habits after 2022.
The shuttle service was cancelled shortly after it began in 2022.
quests.correctAnswer: The new shuttle service appears to have reduced highway congestion by shifting some commuters away from driving.
quests.hint: Track the sequence from no transportation, to the shuttle's introduction, to the survey results and congestion change.
quests.explanation: Following the shuttle's introduction, a third of commuters switched away from driving, and congestion eased on the same highway, together supporting the shuttle as the likely reason for the reduced congestion.
logicChain: Before 2022: no public transit, most residents drive -> 2022: shuttle introduced -> 2023: 30% switch to shuttle, highway congestion eases -> shuttle appears to have reduced congestion by shifting commuters

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct conclusion.
quests.passage: When Elena took over as manager of the downtown branch, customer complaint logs showed an average of eighteen complaints per month, mostly about slow service. She reorganized the staff schedule to add an extra worker during the lunch rush and introduced a new order-tracking system in her second month. By her fourth month, complaints had dropped to six per month, with slow service complaints nearly disappearing, though a few complaints about parking availability remained unchanged.
options: All types of customer complaints disappeared completely after Elena's changes. Such a pattern would remain constant throughout the scenario being described.
Elena's staffing and system changes appear to have specifically reduced complaints about slow service, though not complaints about parking.
Elena's changes caused complaints about parking to increase sharply.
Complaints were already at six per month before Elena became manager. No part of the passage's account suggests otherwise.
quests.correctAnswer: Elena's staffing and system changes appear to have specifically reduced complaints about slow service, though not complaints about parking.
quests.hint: Separate the complaint categories mentioned, and track which ones changed and which stayed the same.
quests.explanation: Slow-service complaints, the specific issue Elena's changes targeted, nearly disappeared, while unrelated parking complaints stayed constant, showing her changes had a targeted effect rather than eliminating every kind of complaint.
logicChain: Before: 18 complaints/month, mostly slow service -> staffing and tracking system changed -> after 4 months: 6 complaints/month, slow-service complaints nearly gone, parking complaints unchanged -> changes appear to have specifically addressed slow service

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct conclusion.
quests.passage: A regional hospital's emergency department tracked patient wait times over eighteen months. In month one, average wait time was 94 minutes. In month six, after the hospital added a fast-track area for minor injuries, average wait time for minor cases dropped to 22 minutes, while wait times for serious cases stayed around 45 minutes throughout the entire period, since the fast-track area was reserved only for minor injuries.
options: The fast-track area reduced wait times equally for both minor and serious cases. This would apply consistently across every detail the passage provides.
Wait times for serious cases also dropped significantly after month six.
The fast-track area was designed to handle only serious injury cases.
The fast-track area appears to have specifically reduced wait times for minor injury cases, without affecting serious case wait times.
quests.correctAnswer: The fast-track area appears to have specifically reduced wait times for minor injury cases, without affecting serious case wait times.
quests.hint: Separate the two categories of cases and track how each one's wait time changed or stayed the same over the eighteen months.
quests.explanation: Minor case wait times dropped sharply only after the fast-track area opened, while serious case wait times stayed constant throughout, since the fast-track area specifically excluded serious cases, showing a targeted rather than universal improvement.
logicChain: Month 1: minor cases wait 94 min -> fast-track area added, minor cases only -> month 6: minor cases wait 22 min -> serious cases: stay ~45 min throughout -> fast-track specifically improved minor case wait times

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct conclusion.
quests.passage: A city library tracked children's summer reading program enrollment over three years. In year one, before any changes, 200 children enrolled. In year two, the library added a prize incentive for finishing five books, and enrollment rose to 340. In year three, the library also began partnering with local schools to distribute flyers directly to students, and enrollment rose again to 610, with school partnership neighborhoods showing the largest jumps.
options: Enrollment declined every year despite the library's new programs. Reading through everything the passage lays out, there is no specific detail that would push against treating this as the straightforward explanation.
Both the prize incentive and the school partnership appear to have contributed to enrollment growth, with the partnership showing an especially strong effect.
The prize incentive had no effect on enrollment numbers at all.
The school partnership was introduced before the prize incentive.
quests.correctAnswer: Both the prize incentive and the school partnership appear to have contributed to enrollment growth, with the partnership showing an especially strong effect.
quests.hint: Track enrollment changes year by year alongside each new initiative introduced.
quests.explanation: Enrollment rose after the prize incentive was added in year two, then rose further after the school partnership began in year three, with that partnership's neighborhoods showing the largest gains, supporting both changes as contributors with the partnership having an especially strong effect.
logicChain: Year 1: 200 enrolled, no changes -> year 2: prize added, 340 enrolled -> year 3: school partnership added, 610 enrolled, partnership areas show largest jumps -> both changes appear to have contributed, partnership especially strongly

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct conclusion.
quests.passage: A mid-size furniture company's customer returns for its flagship sofa averaged 14 percent for years, mostly due to complaints about the fabric wearing thin quickly. In 2021, the company switched to a more durable fabric supplier. In 2022, they also redesigned the packaging to reduce shipping damage. By 2023, returns had dropped to 5 percent, with fabric-related complaints almost entirely gone, while shipping-damage complaints had dropped only slightly, from 3 percent to 2 percent of all orders.
options: The packaging redesign had a larger effect on returns than the fabric change. This would apply consistently across every detail the passage provides.
The new fabric supplier appears to have had the larger effect on reducing returns compared to the packaging redesign.
Fabric-related complaints increased after the supplier was switched. Such a pattern would remain constant throughout the scenario being described.
Both changes were made in the exact same year.
quests.correctAnswer: The new fabric supplier appears to have had the larger effect on reducing returns compared to the packaging redesign.
quests.hint: Separate the two changes by year and compare the size of improvement in each related complaint category.
quests.explanation: Fabric complaints, tied to the 2021 supplier switch, dropped almost entirely, while shipping-damage complaints, tied to the 2022 packaging redesign, dropped only slightly, showing the fabric change had the larger overall effect on returns.
logicChain: Historically: 14% returns, mostly fabric complaints -> 2021: fabric supplier switched -> 2022: packaging redesigned -> 2023: returns at 5%, fabric complaints nearly gone, shipping complaints only slightly down -> fabric change appears to have the larger effect

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct conclusion.

The first update, released in spring, simplified the login process and reduced average login time from 45 seconds to 12 seconds. App store ratings did not change noticeably after this update. options: The bill-pay reminder feature appears more closely linked to the rise in app store ratings than the login simplification.
The login simplification caused the entire rise in app store ratings.
App store ratings dropped after the bill-pay reminder feature was added.
Both updates were released in the same season of the same year.
quests.correctAnswer: The bill-pay reminder feature appears more closely linked to the rise in app store ratings than the login simplification.
quests.hint: Separate the two updates by season and track which one lines up with the ratings change and the specific review mentions.
quests.explanation: Ratings stayed flat after the spring login update but rose sharply after the fall reminder feature, with reviews specifically citing that feature, showing the second update is more closely linked to the improved ratings.
logicChain: Spring: login simplified, ratings unchanged -> fall: bill-pay reminder added, ratings rise 3.2 to 4.1, reviews mention the reminder -> reminder feature appears more closely linked to the ratings increase

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct conclusion.
quests.passage: A university's admissions office tracked application numbers over four years. In year one, before any outreach changes, the school received 4,200 applications. In year two, the office launched a social media campaign targeting prospective students, and applications rose to 4,900. In year three, the office also began offering virtual campus tours, and applications rose again to 6,800, with international applications specifically nearly tripling that year.
options: International applications declined after virtual tours were introduced.
The social media campaign was launched after the virtual tours.
The virtual campus tours appear especially linked to the sharp rise in international applications in year three.
Applications stayed flat across all four years regardless of any changes. The passage offers no detail suggesting this changed over the period discussed.
quests.correctAnswer: The virtual campus tours appear especially linked to the sharp rise in international applications in year three.
quests.hint: Track the two changes by year and notice which specific applicant group showed the sharpest change in year three.
quests.explanation: The virtual tours were introduced in year three, the same year international applications nearly tripled, a group especially likely to benefit from remote access to campus, supporting a specific link between the tours and that group's sharp rise.
logicChain: Year 1: 4,200 applications, no changes -> year 2: social media campaign, 4,900 applications -> year 3: virtual tours added, 6,800 applications, international apps nearly triple -> virtual tours appear especially linked to the international application surge

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct conclusion.
quests.passage: A city's parks department compared usage at two similar-sized parks over one year. Cedar Park added a splash pad in June, and its weekday visitor counts rose from about 80 to 210 people by August, staying elevated through September. Maple Park made no changes during the same period, and its visitor counts stayed steady at around 75 people throughout the summer.
options: Both parks saw the same increase in visitors over the summer.
The splash pad appears specifically linked to Cedar Park's rise in visitors, since the comparable unchanged park saw no similar increase.
Maple Park's visitor counts rose more than Cedar Park's.
Cedar Park's visitor increase happened before the splash pad was installed.
quests.correctAnswer: The splash pad appears specifically linked to Cedar Park's rise in visitors, since the comparable unchanged park saw no similar increase.
quests.hint: Compare Cedar Park's timeline and outcome to Maple Park's, since Maple Park serves as an unchanged comparison.
quests.explanation: Cedar Park's visitor count nearly tripled after the splash pad's June installation and stayed elevated, while the similar, unchanged Maple Park saw no such increase, strengthening the case that the splash pad specifically drove Cedar Park's growth.
logicChain: Cedar Park: splash pad added in June -> visitors rise from 80 to 210 by August, stay elevated -> Maple Park: no changes -> visitors stay ~75 all summer -> splash pad appears specifically linked to Cedar Park's increase

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct conclusion.
quests.passage: A software company tracked customer support ticket volume after launching two features in the same quarter: an in-app help center in April, and a live chat option in May. Tickets related to 'how do I' questions dropped sharply after the help center launched. options: Each new feature appears linked to a drop in a different specific category of support tickets, based on when each was introduced.
Both features were launched at the same time in April.
The help center reduced urgent account issue tickets specifically.
Neither feature had any effect on support ticket volume.
quests.correctAnswer: Each new feature appears linked to a drop in a different specific category of support tickets, based on when each was introduced.
quests.hint: Track each feature by its launch month and match it to the specific ticket category that changed afterward.
quests.explanation: 'How do I' tickets dropped right after the April help center launch, while urgent issue tickets dropped only after the May live chat launch, showing each feature aligns with its own specific category of improvement rather than one feature explaining both.
logicChain: April: help center launches -> 'how do I' tickets drop -> May: live chat launches -> urgent account tickets drop -> each feature appears linked to its own specific ticket category

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct conclusion.
quests.passage: A regional grocery chain compared two pilot programs across different store groups. Group A stores introduced self-checkout lanes, and average checkout wait times dropped from 6 minutes to 3 minutes, while customer complaints about long lines dropped from 22 percent to 9 percent of surveys. Group B stores instead added more staffed registers during peak hours, and wait times dropped from 6 minutes to 4 minutes, with complaints dropping from 22 percent to 14 percent.
options: Group B's staffed registers had a larger effect than Group A's self-checkout lanes. The way the events are described throughout the passage offers no clear signal that this particular reading should be treated with any extra caution.

Neither pilot program had any effect on wait times or complaints. As far as the passage's description goes, nothing about the surrounding details would suggest this needs to be treated as an incomplete picture.
Both groups saw identical results from their respective changes.
The self-checkout lanes in Group A appear to have had a somewhat larger effect on reducing wait times and complaints than adding staffed registers in Group B.
quests.correctAnswer: The self-checkout lanes in Group A appear to have had a somewhat larger effect on reducing wait times and complaints than adding staffed registers in Group B.
quests.hint: Compare the size of the improvement in both wait times and complaints across the two groups.
quests.explanation: Group A's self-checkout lanes produced a larger drop in both wait time (6 to 3 minutes) and complaints (22 to 9 percent) compared to Group B's staffed registers (6 to 4 minutes, 22 to 14 percent), showing a somewhat stronger overall effect.
logicChain: Group A: self-checkout added -> wait time 6 to 3 min, complaints 22% to 9% -> Group B: staffed registers added -> wait time 6 to 4 min, complaints 22% to 14% -> Group A's change shows a somewhat larger improvement

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct conclusion.
quests.passage: A city's animal shelter tracked adoption rates over two years. In year one, before any changes, the shelter had an adoption rate of 45 percent for cats and 60 percent for dogs. In year two, the shelter began featuring animals in short videos on social media instead of only photos. By the end of year two, the cat adoption rate rose to 68 percent, while the dog adoption rate rose slightly to 64 percent.
options: The video feature had an identical effect on both cat and dog adoption rates.
Dog adoption rates rose more than cat adoption rates after the videos began.
The video feature appears to have had a much larger effect on cat adoptions than on dog adoptions.
Cat adoption rates dropped after the shelter began using videos.
quests.correctAnswer: The video feature appears to have had a much larger effect on cat adoptions than on dog adoptions.
quests.hint: Compare the size of the change in cat adoption rates to the size of the change in dog adoption rates.
quests.explanation: Cat adoptions jumped 23 percentage points while dog adoptions rose only 4 points after the same video feature was introduced, showing the change had a much stronger effect specifically for cats.
logicChain: Year 1: cats 45%, dogs 60% adopted -> year 2: videos introduced -> cats rise to 68% (+23 pts), dogs rise to 64% (+4 pts) -> video feature appears to have had a much larger effect on cat adoptions

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct conclusion.
quests.passage: A manufacturing plant tracked defect rates for two product lines after installing new quality-control cameras on the assembly line. For Product Line A, which involves simple assembly steps, defect rates dropped from 4 percent to 1 percent within a month. For Product Line B, which involves more complex assembly with many small parts, defect rates dropped only from 6 percent to 5 percent over the same period.
options: The new cameras appear to have been more effective at catching defects in the simpler assembly process than the more complex one.
The cameras were more effective for Product Line B than Product Line A.
Defect rates increased for both product lines after the cameras were installed.
The cameras had no measurable effect on either product line.

quests.hint: Compare the size of the defect rate drop for each product line relative to its complexity.
quests.explanation: Product Line A's defect rate dropped by three percentage points while Product Line B's dropped by only one, suggesting the cameras worked better for the simpler process, possibly because complex assembly with many small parts is harder to monitor visually.
logicChain: Product A (simple assembly): defects 4% to 1% -> Product B (complex assembly): defects 6% to 5% -> cameras appear more effective for the simpler process than the more complex one

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct conclusion.
quests.passage: A city's recycling program tracked participation in two types of neighborhoods after distributing informational brochures. In neighborhoods with curbside recycling bins already in place, participation rose from 55 percent to 71 percent after the brochures arrived. options: The brochures had a larger effect in neighborhoods without curbside bins.
Participation dropped in both types of neighborhoods after the brochures arrived.
Both types of neighborhoods showed identical increases in participation.
The brochures appear to have had a much larger effect in neighborhoods that already had convenient curbside bins.

quests.explanation: Curbside neighborhoods saw a 16-point rise in participation compared to just a 4-point rise in drop-off neighborhoods, suggesting the brochures were more effective where the physical convenience of recycling was already in place.
logicChain: Curbside neighborhoods: participation 55% to 71% (+16 pts) -> drop-off neighborhoods: 20% to 24% (+4 pts) -> brochures appear to have had a much larger effect where curbside convenience already existed

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct conclusion.

At Hub A, which had the oldest gate infrastructure and frequent equipment issues, complaints dropped only slightly, from 12 percent to 10 percent of flights. options: The standardized announcements were most effective at the hub with the oldest infrastructure. No part of the passage's account suggests otherwise.
Complaints increased at all three hubs after the announcements were standardized.
The standardized announcements appear less effective at reducing complaints at the hub with older, less reliable infrastructure.
All three hubs showed identical improvement after the change.

quests.hint: Compare Hub A's outcome to Hubs B and C's outcome, and consider what's different about Hub A's infrastructure.
quests.explanation: Hubs with newer infrastructure saw complaints drop by two-thirds, while the hub with older infrastructure and equipment issues saw only a small improvement, suggesting infrastructure problems may be limiting how much the announcement change alone can help.
logicChain: Hub A (old infrastructure, frequent equipment issues): complaints 12% to 10% -> Hubs B and C (newer infrastructure): complaints 12% to 4% each -> announcements appear less effective where infrastructure issues remain

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct conclusion.
quests.passage: A hospital tracked nurse overtime hours after introducing a new scheduling algorithm on two of its five floors. On the medical-surgical floor, where patient needs are relatively predictable, overtime hours dropped from 340 to 90 hours per month. On the intensive care floor, where patient needs fluctuate rapidly and unpredictably, overtime hours dropped only from 310 to 260 hours per month.
options: The algorithm was more effective on the intensive care floor than the medical-surgical floor.
Overtime hours increased on both floors after the algorithm was introduced.
Both floors showed identical reductions in overtime hours.
The new algorithm appears more effective at reducing overtime on floors with more predictable patient needs.

quests.hint: Compare the size of the overtime reduction on each floor, and consider how predictable each floor's patient needs are.
quests.explanation: The medical-surgical floor, with more predictable needs, saw overtime drop by 250 hours, while the intensive care floor, with unpredictable needs, saw only a 50-hour drop, suggesting the algorithm works better when patient demand is easier to forecast.
logicChain: Medical-surgical floor (predictable needs): overtime 340 to 90 hrs -> ICU floor (unpredictable needs): overtime 310 to 260 hrs -> algorithm appears more effective where patient needs are more predictable

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct conclusion.
quests.passage: A national retailer tracked online sales after redesigning its website's checkout process. For customers using desktop computers, the redesign reduced cart abandonment from 68 percent to 41 percent. For customers using mobile phones, cart abandonment dropped only from 74 percent to 66 percent, and the company's data team noted the new checkout page still loaded slowly on many mobile devices.

The redesign appears less effective for mobile users, possibly due to slow loading times on mobile devices.
Cart abandonment increased for both desktop and mobile users after the redesign, according to how the passage describes the situation.
Mobile loading speed had no possible connection to the abandonment rates. The passage offers no detail suggesting this changed over the period discussed.
quests.correctAnswer: The redesign appears less effective for mobile users, possibly due to slow loading times on mobile devices.
quests.hint: Compare the size of improvement for desktop versus mobile, and note the detail about mobile loading speed.
quests.explanation: Desktop abandonment dropped much more sharply than mobile abandonment, and the passage specifically notes slow mobile loading times, supporting the idea that loading speed may be limiting the redesign's effectiveness on mobile.
logicChain: Desktop: cart abandonment 68% to 41% -> mobile: 74% to 66%, still loads slowly -> redesign appears less effective for mobile, possibly due to slow loading times

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct conclusion.

In Complex B, where residents had to manually enable energy-saving settings themselves, only 22 percent of residents did so, and overall building energy usage dropped by just 5 percent.
options: Requiring residents to opt in manually led to greater energy savings.

All residents in Complex B chose to enable the energy-saving settings.
Making the energy-saving setting the default appears to have led to greater overall energy savings than requiring residents to opt in manually.

quests.hint: Compare the two complexes' approaches to enabling the setting and their resulting overall savings.
quests.explanation: Complex A's default energy-saving setting produced a much larger building-wide reduction than Complex B's opt-in approach, where only a fifth of residents actually enabled it, suggesting the default setting was more effective at achieving overall savings.
logicChain: Complex A: energy-saving mode set as default -> usage drops 19% -> Complex B: residents must opt in, only 22% do -> usage drops 5% -> default setting appears more effective for overall savings

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct conclusion.
quests.passage: A school district compared reading scores after introducing a new phonics-based curriculum in half its elementary schools, chosen because those schools had the lowest reading scores the year before. A year later, the phonics schools' average reading scores rose from 58 to 74, while the schools that kept the old curriculum, which already had higher starting scores, rose slightly from 79 to 82.

The phonics-based curriculum appears linked to substantial improvement, though the schools using it started from a lower baseline.
The old curriculum produced a larger improvement than the new phonics curriculum.
Both groups of schools started with identical reading scores.

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct conclusion.

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct conclusion.

'The Garden Party' sold more tickets than 'Midnight Run.'

quests.hint: Notice both the marketing difference and the additional detail about the lead actor, and avoid crediting only one factor with certainty.
quests.explanation: While the marketing approach differed and sales were higher for 'Midnight Run,' the passage also notes its more well-known lead actor, meaning both factors are plausible contributors rather than the marketing method alone explaining the difference with certainty.
logicChain: 'The Garden Party': newspaper ads -> 62% seats sold -> 'Midnight Run': social media ads, also more famous lead -> 89% seats sold -> social media and the actor's fame both appear as plausible contributors

options: The traditional patching method is definitely more durable than the sealing method, given the way the passage frames things.
The newer method costs less than the traditional patching method.
The newer sealing method appears more durable, though it comes with a higher cost trade-off.
Both methods showed identical durability results.

quests.hint: Weigh both the durability outcome and the cost detail mentioned for the newer method.
quests.explanation: The sealing method lasted nearly three times longer than traditional patching, but the passage also notes it costs more, supporting a conclusion that reflects both the durability benefit and its cost trade-off.
logicChain: Traditional patching: re-repair needed in ~8 months -> newer sealing method: re-repair needed in ~22 months, costs 40% more -> newer method appears more durable, with a cost trade-off

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct conclusion.
quests.passage: A national coffee chain compared customer wait times after redesigning its mobile ordering system. For customers ordering simple drinks like plain coffee, average wait time dropped from 6 minutes to 2 minutes.
